questions.q: If a classroom has 10 boys and 15 girls, what is the ratio of boys to girls in its simplest form?
questions.a: The ratio is 2:3. A wrong answer like 10:15 suggests the student doesn't know how to simplify ratios by dividing both sides by a common factor (in this case, 5).

questions.q: Are the ratios 3:4 and 9:12 equivalent? Explain why or why not.
questions.a: Yes, they are equivalent. A wrong answer suggests the student is looking at the numbers as separate entities rather than a relationship, failing to see that 3x3=9 and 4x3=12, keeping the proportion constant.

questions.q: A map scale is 1:1000. If two towns are 5 cm apart on the map, what is the actual distance in metres?
questions.a: The actual distance is 5000 cm, which is 50 metres. A wrong answer often ignores the unit conversion or fails to multiply the map distance by the scale factor, indicating confusion between map units and real-world units.

questions.q: If 5 notebooks cost 100 rupees, how much will 8 notebooks cost?
questions.a: Each notebook costs 20 rupees, so 8 notebooks cost 160 rupees. A wrong answer indicates the student is not finding the "unit rate" first or fails to set up the proportion correctly (5:100 = 8:x).

questions.q: Can you have a ratio between 5 apples and 3 kilograms of rice? Why or why not?
questions.a: No, because ratios compare quantities of the same kind. A wrong answer shows the student does not understand that ratio requires a common unit of measure (e.g., you cannot compare "count" to "weight" directly as a ratio).

questions.q: Create a real-world scenario where the ratio of two items must remain constant.
questions.a: A good answer involves recipes, fuel consumption, or salary/wage calculations where increasing one part requires increasing the other proportionately. A poor answer gives an example where variables change independently, like a child's age versus their height.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Ratio is a ______ way of comparing two quantities of the same kind by division, showing how many times one quantity contains the other.
Fill in the blank: Start by writing the ______ as a ratio: 2 cups : 4 people.
What is Ratio? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Ratio is a mathematical way of comparing two quantities of the same kind by division, showing how many times one quantity contains the other.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Ratio?
questions.a: Students often try to solve proportion problems by adding the same number to both sides of a ratio instead of multiplying/dividing.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to express a real-world comparison as a ratio and set up an equation to find a missing value in a proportional relationship.
